intro: You are Maria Skłodowska, a top student in a Warsaw where Polish is suppressed and women may not enter university. Doors are locked by law, so you study in secret, then in Paris, and then in a leaky shed full of ore.

ladder.why: Education: in Russian-ruled Warsaw women were barred from university and Polish was banned.

office.why: Institutions: the Academy of Sciences refused to admit her by a narrow vote.

market.why: Press and public: in 1911 newspapers attacked her with sexist and xenophobic language.

bridge.why: Partnership: Pierre insisted that she be named with him for the Nobel Prize.

advantage.title: Method and notebooks
advantage.text: Curie solved problems by careful measurement and by ruling out what could not be true. Use it to remove one wrong answer before you decide.

life.title: Warsaw, 1867
life.text: Maria is born on 7 November 1867, the youngest of five children of two teachers. Poland is ruled by Russia, and Polish language and history are banned from the classroom.

life.title: Loss at ten
life.text: Her sister Zofia dies of typhus in 1876 and her mother of tuberculosis in 1878. Her father loses his post for his Polish views, so money is short for the whole family.

life.title: Gold medal at fifteen
life.text: Maria finishes school as the best in her class and receives a gold medal. Her parents, both teachers, had made learning the centre of the home.

life.title: A university that says no
life.text: The University of Warsaw does not accept women. Maria and her sister Bronisława study at the secret "Flying University" and agree to take turns: Maria works first so Bronisława can study medicine in Paris.

life.title: The Flying University
life.text: Teachers moved from flat to flat so that women could be taught without police noticing. Maria learned science and also taught others.

q.q: What was the "Flying University" in Warsaw?
a: A secret school where women could study
A university that taught on trains
q.x: It was an underground school for Polish women, held in private flats and moved often because Russian authorities did not allow it.

life.title: Paris, 1891
life.text: At 24 Maria enrols at the Sorbonne as "Marie". She lives in a cold attic and sometimes forgets to eat, but passes physics in 1893 and mathematics in 1894.

life.title: A partner in the lab
life.text: In 1895 Marie marries the physicist Pierre Curie. They share ideas, notes and work as equals, and later write their results under both names.

life.title: Polonium and radium
life.text: In 1898 Marie and Pierre announce two new elements. She coins the word "radioactivity". They work in a leaky shed and process tons of ore by hand.

q.q: Marie named one new element after her homeland. Which?
q.x: Polonium is named for Poland, which did not exist as an independent state when she named it in 1898.

life.title: Nobel Prize, 1903
life.text: Marie and Pierre share the Nobel Prize in Physics with Henri Becquerel. She is the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. They choose not to patent their method so that other scientists can use it.

life.title: Alone, then in the headlines
life.text: Pierre is killed in a street accident in 1906, and Marie takes over his chair as the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 the French Academy rejects her narrowly and the press attacks her as a foreigner.

life.title: The Little Curies
life.text: In 1911 she also wins a second Nobel Prize, in Chemistry. In the First World War she equips vehicles with X-ray machines and trains women to run them, so surgeons can find bullets and shrapnel.

life.title: A lab for the world
life.text: Marie builds the Radium Institute in Paris and trains many researchers, many of them women. Her daughter Irène wins the Chemistry Nobel in 1935. Marie dies in 1934, probably of radiation exposure.

sources: Nobel Prize site: Marie Curie biographical
flags: Check wording that the 1911 Academy vote was narrowly lost, and that the Flying University used private flats and rotating teachers.
Dates for Pierre's 1906 chair and the first woman professor at the Sorbonne were taken from the single-player data.

evidence.ev: Warsaw was under Russian rule: Polish was suppressed in schools, and women could not attend university.
She joined the secret Flying University in Warsaw, where Polish women studied in private flats.
She enrolled at the Sorbonne in Paris in 1891 and earned degrees in physics and mathematics.
With Pierre she processed tonnes of pitchblende in a leaky shed to isolate radium.
The French Academy of Sciences narrowly voted against her membership in 1911; it elected its first woman full member only in 1979.
A press campaign around the Langevin affair attacked her, often with xenophobic and sexist language.
Pierre made sure she was named with him for the Nobel Prize in Physics after the first nomination left her out.
